Yes, the story has an appropriate and effective balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer uses real-time scenes to anchor the narrative—such as Hollis discovering the wrecked car, speaking with the 911 dispatcher, talking aloud to the deceased woman while waiting, and interacting with the deputy when help finally arrives. Interwoven seamlessly within these quiet scenes are brief passages of summary and exposition that provide essential background information about Hollis's solitude, his thirty-one years as a surveyor, his estranged daughter, and his late ex-wife. Because the story takes place over nearly four hours of Hollis sitting alone in the woods, compressing time with exposition and internal reflection keeps the pacing steady and enriches the emotional weight of the real-time vigil without letting the story become either bogged down or dry.
